S13v10-2P1P2:
Have you noticed people often choose their community in the same way they would choose a vacation rental? “Wow! Look at this beautiful land! And a pond, with the sunset in it!! Who needs a beach?! And the people seem really nice, let’s get in here!” Fast forward two years. “Wait, there’s a vaccination policy?? And you need paperwork for it?!?!”

When you go to visit a community, have a list ready of what you really believe about children, money, property ownership, romance, medicine, food, spiritual practice, technology, privacy, conflict and leaving. Where are you still unsure? Mark those places too.
S13v10-2P3: Throw sexuality and gender onto that list. Yes, it keeps getting longer. Could an LGBTQ+ member live openly there? Date and/or be in a relationship? Would the community keep them fully protected? Should children be taught to question their sexual identities at an early age? Should one of the children grow up to be gay or transgender, what happens then? Until a group has answered these questions, its values on freedom and child-rearing are incomplete.

Willing to experiment? That's a real value too! Make sure that your list declares whether or not you value experimenting, because the folks next to you may think experimenting ended in 1978 and anything that came from it is doctrine now.
S13v10-2P4: Once you’ve got a good sense of what is important to you, compare this to how the group actually functions (not just how they talk about it in public). How was a recent conflict handled? Who can block decisions? How did it go for the last person who left the group? Who owns the land? It’ll be uncomfortable to have these conversations, but the view won’t go away after you’ve had them.

S13v10-5P2: That said, the power to remove somebody is also one of the easiest powers to abuse. So work out the process before it's about anyone in particular. What conduct constitutes a reason for immediate protective action, and who decides on temporary restrictions? Who preserves the evidence, and who has to step aside from the decisions? How does the person reply, and what review or appeal is possible without endangering others? How do people who are separated get housed, have their records and family connections protected, and still be able to use common resources or have access to outside funds, if any? When do people reach for outside help? (More on that one next.)
S13v10-5P4: Also pick a mediator or ombud beforehand. Why bother? Because if they are chosen in a crisis, and nobody has met this “neutral stranger” before, people often do not trust them. And remember that although mediation is for repairing relations, it does not replace the need for evidence, safeguarding or a ruling. And it does not replace the finality of separation once someone no longer consents to the shared life.
